# Old Tax Regime vs New Tax Regime for Salaried Employees in India (FY 2026-27): Which One Saves More Tax?


October 15, 2026


[Shashank Yadav](https://salarybox.in/blog/author/shashank87cc9f270b/)


[No comments yet](https://salarybox.in/blog/old-tax-regime-vs-new-tax-regime-for-salaried-employees-in-india-fy-2026-27-which-one-saves-more-tax/#respond)


“Should I choose the old tax regime or the new one?”


This is the single most asked tax question by salaried employees in India. Every year, during investment declaration season, millions of employees stare at the form their HR department sends and wonder which box to tick.


The answer is not the same for everyone. It depends on your salary level, where you live, whether you have a home loan, how much you invest in tax saving instruments, and whether you pay rent. At certain salary levels, the new regime wins by a wide margin. At others, the old regime can save you lakhs.


This guide gives you a clear, number by number comparison at multiple salary levels so you can make the right choice for FY 2026-27 (AY 2027-28). No vague advice. Just tables with actual rupee amounts.


## **What Changed for FY 2026-27?**


Before diving into comparisons, let us address the biggest question: did anything change this year?


**Item** **FY 2025-26** **FY 2026-27** **Changed?**


New Regime Tax Slabs 0% to 30% in 7 slabs Same No


Old Regime Tax Slabs 0%, 5%, 20%, 30% Same No


Standard Deduction (New Regime) ₹75,000 ₹75,000 No


Standard Deduction (Old Regime) ₹50,000 ₹50,000 No


Section 87A Rebate (New Regime) ₹60,000 (income up to ₹12 lakh) ₹60,000 (income up to ₹12 lakh) No


Section 87A Rebate (Old Regime) ₹12,500 (income up to ₹5 lakh) ₹12,500 (income up to ₹5 lakh) No


Section 80C Limit ₹1,50,000 ₹1,50,000 No


Section 80D Limit ₹25,000 / ₹50,000 ₹25,000 / ₹50,000 No


HRA Exemption Rules Available in old regime Same No


Governing Law Income Tax Act, 1961 Income Tax Act, 2025 Yes (new act, same rates)


Default Regime New Regime New Regime No


ITR Filing Deadline July 31 July 31 No


Revised Return Window 9 months from end of AY 12 months from end of AY Yes


**Key takeaway:** The tax slabs, deductions, and exemptions are identical to last year. The Income Tax Act, 2025 replaced the 1961 Act from April 1, 2026, but the section numbers changed while the deduction principles and amounts stayed the same. So your calculation from last year still holds.


## **Tax Slabs: Side by Side Comparison**


### **New Tax Regime (Default) for FY 2026-27**


**Income Slab** **Tax Rate**


Up to ₹4,00,000 Nil


₹4,00,001 to ₹8,00,000 5%


₹8,00,001 to ₹12,00,000 10%


₹12,00,001 to ₹16,00,000 15%


₹16,00,001 to ₹20,00,000 20%


₹20,00,001 to ₹24,00,000 25%


Above ₹24,00,000 30%


**Plus:** 4% Health and Education Cess on total tax
**Rebate:** Section 87A rebate of ₹60,000 if total income does not exceed ₹12,00,000
**Effective zero tax:** Salary up to ₹12,75,000 (₹12 lakh + ₹75,000 standard deduction)
**Surcharge cap:** Maximum surcharge is 25% (even for income above ₹5 crore)


### **Old Tax Regime for FY 2026-27**


**Income Slab** **Tax Rate**


Up to ₹2,50,000 Nil


₹2,50,001 to ₹5,00,000 5%


₹5,00,001 to ₹10,00,000 20%


Above ₹10,00,000 30%


**Plus:** 4% Health and Education Cess on total tax
**Rebate:** Section 87A rebate of ₹12,500 if total income does not exceed ₹5,00,000
**Effective zero tax:** Salary up to approximately ₹5,50,000 (₹5 lakh + ₹50,000 standard deduction)
**Surcharge:** Up to 37% for income above ₹5 crore


### **Visual Slab Comparison**


**Income Level** **Old Regime Rate** **New Regime Rate** **Which Is Lower?**

₹20,00,000 30% 20% New


₹25,00,000 30% 30% Same


Looking at slabs alone, the new regime wins at almost every income level. The old regime catches up only when you add deductions and exemptions. That is the real comparison we need to make.


## **Deductions and Exemptions: What Is Available Where?**


This is the most important table in this entire guide. The old regime’s advantage comes entirely from the deductions and exemptions it allows. The new regime offers simplicity with lower slab rates but strips away most deductions.


### **Deductions Available ONLY in the Old Regime**

Section 80D Health insurance premium (self and family) ₹25,000 (₹50,000 for senior citizens)


Section 80D Health insurance for parents ₹25,000 (₹50,000 if parents are senior citizens)


Section 80E Education loan interest No limit (full interest amount)

Section 80U Individual with disability ₹75,000 or ₹1,25,000


Section 10(13A) HRA Exemption Based on formula


Section 10(5) Leave Travel Allowance Actual travel expenses


Section 24(b) Home Loan Interest (self occupied) ₹2,00,000


Section 24(b) Home Loan Interest (let out) No limit


### **Deductions Available in BOTH Regimes**


**Deduction** **Old Regime** **New Regime**

### **Maximum Possible Deductions Under Old Regime**


For a salaried employee making full use of all available deductions:


**Deduction** **Annual Amount**


Standard Deduction ₹50,000


Section 80C (full limit) ₹1,50,000


Section 80CCD(1B) (NPS) ₹50,000


Section 80D (self + parents, all below 60) ₹50,000

Very few employees actually claim all of these. Most salaried individuals claim Standard Deduction, Section 80C, Section 80D, and possibly HRA or home loan interest. The typical realistic deduction range is ₹2,50,000 to ₹4,50,000.

Section 87A Rebate ₹0 (income exceeds ₹5 lakh) ₹16,125 (income below ₹12 lakh)

**Total Tax Payable** **₹28,080** **₹0**


**Winner at ₹8 LPA:** New Regime by ₹28,080. The new regime gives you zero tax thanks to the Section 87A rebate, while the old regime taxes you because your income exceeds the ₹5 lakh rebate threshold even after deductions.

**Total Tax Payable** **₹44,720** **₹0**


**Winner at ₹10 LPA:** New Regime by ₹44,720. Even with ₹3,47,500 in total deductions under the old regime, the new regime wins because its ₹12 lakh rebate threshold wipes out the entire tax liability.

## **The Breakeven Table: How Much Deduction Makes Old Regime Win?**


This is the most useful table in this guide. It tells you exactly how much in deductions (beyond standard deduction) you need to claim under the old regime to make it cheaper than the new regime.


**Gross Salary** **New Regime Tax (₹)** **Breakeven Deduction Needed in Old Regime** **Realistic to Achieve?**


₹6,00,000 ₹0 Not applicable (both are zero tax) N/A


₹8,00,000 ₹0 ₹2,50,000+ Very difficult (rebate gap too large)


₹10,00,000 ₹0 ₹4,50,000+ Nearly impossible


₹12,75,000 ₹0 ₹7,25,000+ Impossible


₹15,00,000 ₹97,110 ₹3,25,000 to ₹5,50,000 Possible with home loan


₹20,00,000 ₹1,91,880 ₹7,00,000 to ₹7,50,000 Difficult


₹25,00,000 ₹3,19,800 ₹8,00,000+ Very difficult


₹30,00,000 ₹4,75,020 ₹8,00,000+ Nearly impossible


**The pattern is clear:** For salary up to ₹12,75,000, the new regime wins every time because the Section 87A rebate makes your tax zero. Between ₹13 lakh and ₹18 lakh, the old regime can win if you have a home loan plus full 80C and HRA claims. Above ₹20 lakh, the deduction caps under the old regime make it extremely difficult to beat the new regime.


## **Decision Framework: Which Regime Should You Choose?**


### **Quick Decision Flowchart**


**Your Situation** **Recommended Regime** **Reason**


Gross salary up to ₹12,75,000 New Regime Zero tax regardless of deductions


Salary ₹13L to ₹18L, no home loan, low deductions (below ₹2L) New Regime Lower slab rates win easily


Salary ₹13L to ₹18L, home loan + full 80C + HRA claim Old Regime Total deductions cross ₹5.5 lakh breakeven


Salary ₹13L to ₹18L, home loan but no HRA (own house) Case by case Depends on exact deduction total


Salary above ₹20L, no home loan New Regime Cannot reach ₹7L+ deductions without home loan


Salary above ₹20L, with home loan + HRA + full 80C + 80D + NPS Compare carefully Close contest, calculate both


Salary above ₹50L New Regime usually 25% surcharge cap vs 37% in old regime


You do not want to track investments New Regime Zero paperwork, zero proof submission


### **The Home Loan Factor**


Home loan interest deduction (Section 24(b)) is the single biggest swing factor. It can shift the comparison by ₹40,000 to ₹60,000 in tax savings under the old regime.


**Home Loan Scenario** **Interest Paid Annually** **Deduction Under Old Regime** **Available in New Regime?**


Self occupied property, loan up to ₹35 lakh ₹2,50,000 to ₹3,50,000 ₹2,00,000 (capped) No


Self occupied property, loan above ₹35 lakh ₹3,50,000+ ₹2,00,000 (capped) No


Let out property ₹2,50,000 to ₹5,00,000 Full interest (no cap) No


Pre construction interest Up to ₹2,00,000 (in 5 installments) ₹40,000 per year for 5 years No


**Note:** If you own a home and have an active home loan, the old regime almost always deserves a serious look. The ₹2 lakh interest deduction plus ₹1.5 lakh principal under 80C (total ₹3.5 lakh from home loan alone) is a powerful combination that the new regime simply cannot match.


### **The HRA Factor**


HRA exemption is the second biggest swing factor, especially for employees living in metro cities and paying high rent.


**Monthly Rent** **City Type** **Approximate Annual HRA Exemption** **Conditions**


₹10,000 Metro ₹72,000 to ₹96,000 Depends on basic salary and actual HRA received


₹15,000 Metro ₹1,08,000 to ₹1,44,000 Higher basic = higher exemption


₹20,000 Metro ₹1,44,000 to ₹1,92,000 Must have rent receipts


₹25,000 Metro ₹1,80,000 to ₹2,40,000 Landlord PAN required if rent exceeds ₹1 lakh/year


₹30,000 Metro ₹2,16,000 to ₹3,00,000 Only available in old regime


₹10,000 Non-metro ₹48,000 to ₹72,000 40% of basic (vs 50% for metro)


₹15,000 Non-metro ₹72,000 to ₹1,08,000 Lower exemption than metro


**HRA Exemption is calculated as the minimum of three amounts:**


1. Actual HRA received from employer
2. Rent paid minus 10% of basic salary
3. 50% of basic salary (metro cities: Mumbai, Delhi, Chennai, Kolkata) or 40% of basic salary (other cities)


If you live in your own house or do not pay rent, HRA exemption is zero, which significantly weakens the case for the old regime.

### **What Happens If You Chose Wrong?**


If you informed your employer that you want the old regime but realize at ITR filing time that the new regime saves more tax, you can simply select the new regime while filing your ITR. Your employer will have deducted TDS based on the old regime (likely higher TDS), so you will get the excess TDS refunded when the ITR is processed.


Similarly, if you chose the new regime with your employer but want to file under the old regime, you can do so at ITR filing time (only for salaried employees; business owners face restrictions).

## **Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)**


**1. Which tax regime is better for a salary of ₹10 lakh in FY 2026-27?**


The new tax regime is clearly better for a ₹10 lakh salary. Under the new regime, after the ₹75,000 standard deduction, your taxable income becomes ₹9,25,000, which is below the ₹12 lakh Section 87A rebate threshold. This means your tax is zero. Under the old regime, even with ₹1,50,000 in Section 80C and ₹25,000 in Section 80D deductions, your taxable income would be around ₹6,72,500, resulting in a tax of approximately ₹36,660. The new regime saves you this entire amount with no investment requirements.


**2. Can I switch between old and new tax regime every year?**


Yes, salaried employees can switch between the old and new tax regime every financial year. There is no restriction on how many times you switch. You inform your employer at the start of the year for TDS calculation purposes, but the final choice is made when you file your ITR. Even if you told your employer one regime, you can select the other when filing your return. For business owners, the rules are different. They can opt out of the new regime once by filing Form 10-IEA, and if they switch back to the new regime, they cannot opt out again.


**3. What deductions are available under the new tax regime?**


The new regime allows very limited deductions. You get the ₹75,000 standard deduction, professional tax deduction (up to ₹2,500), employer NPS contribution under Section 80CCD(2) up to 14% of basic plus DA, gratuity exemption, leave encashment exemption, VRS exemption up to ₹5 lakh, and transport allowance for disabled employees. All major deductions like Section 80C, 80D, HRA exemption, home loan interest under Section 24(b), 80CCD(1B) NPS, and LTA are not available.


**4. I pay ₹20,000 rent per month. Should I choose the old regime for HRA exemption?**


It depends entirely on your salary level and total deductions. If your gross salary is below ₹12,75,000, the new regime gives you zero tax regardless of HRA, so the new regime is better. If your salary is between ₹13 lakh and ₹18 lakh, the HRA exemption (approximately ₹1,44,000 to ₹1,92,000 annually for ₹20,000 rent in a metro city) combined with 80C, 80D, and other deductions may or may not cross the breakeven point. You need to calculate with your exact salary structure. Above ₹20 lakh, HRA alone is unlikely to tip the scale unless you also have a home loan and full Chapter VI-A deductions.


**5. Is the old tax regime being removed or phased out?**


No. As of FY 2026-27, both regimes continue to exist. The new regime is the default (meaning if you do not actively choose, the new regime applies), but the old regime remains fully available. The government has not announced any plans to discontinue the old regime. However, since FY 2020-21, all enhancements (higher rebate threshold, wider slabs, higher standard deduction) have been made only to the new regime, which suggests the government is gradually making the new regime more attractive.


**6. How does the Section 87A rebate work differently in each regime?**


Under the new regime, the Section 87A rebate is ₹60,000, which wipes out tax for individuals with total income up to ₹12,00,000. With the ₹75,000 standard deduction, the effective zero tax threshold for salaried employees is ₹12,75,000. Marginal relief is also available for income slightly above ₹12 lakh, meaning your tax will not exceed the amount by which your income exceeds ₹12 lakh. Under the old regime, the rebate is only ₹12,500 for income up to ₹5,00,000, making the effective zero tax threshold approximately ₹5,50,000 (with ₹50,000 standard deduction). This massive gap in rebate amounts is the primary reason the new regime dominates at salary levels up to ₹12.75 lakh.


**7. My employer offers NPS. Does that help in the new regime?**


Yes. Employer NPS contribution under Section 80CCD(2) is one of the few deductions available in both regimes. In fact, the cap is more generous in the new regime: 14% of basic plus DA for all employees (private and government), compared to 10% for private sector employees under the old regime (government employees get 14% in both). If your basic salary is ₹6,00,000 per year, your employer can contribute up to ₹84,000 to NPS, and this amount is deductible from your taxable income even under the new regime. Ask your employer if they offer NPS as part of the salary structure.


**8. I have both a home loan and pay rent (I rent in a different city from where my property is). Which regime should I choose?**


This is one of the rare situations where the old regime almost always wins. You can claim HRA exemption for the rent you pay (if the rented property is in a different city from your owned property), home loan interest deduction under Section 24(b) for the property you own, home loan principal repayment under Section 80C, and all other Chapter VI-A deductions. Combined deductions in this scenario easily cross ₹5 lakh to ₹8 lakh, making the old regime substantially cheaper. Calculate both options with your exact numbers, but the old regime is likely your answer.
